title: Crossing the Line: Simulation and Boundary Areas
source_display_name: Simulation in Healthcare The Journal of the Society for Simulation in Healthcare
abstract: These are challenging times for the simulation community—times of uncertainty, of ferment, and of rapid growth. This instability reflects the realities of healthcare and healthcare education, where traditional approaches to training are no longer possible. By offering safe, learner-centered training, simulation occupies a central position. If simulation is to be fit for purpose, we need to elaborate an underpinning “theory of simulation.” As well as establishing the scientific basis of our field, this will provide insight into the theoretical frameworks of related disciplines, helping learners and teachers to select the type of simulation which best meets their needs at a given moment. Effective simulation interweaves clinical practice, laboratory science, education, computer design and many other disciplines. This richness and diversity is a key strength, bringing creativity and innovation and presenting teachers and learners with a wide choice. Yet there is a danger that this very diversity may lead to fragmentation and a lack of overall direction. Without a coherent theory, it is easy to get lost in a confusion of beguiling but disparate fields. In this paper, I frame simulation as a conceptual space where many domains come into contact. Drawing on personal experience, observation and my reading of the literature, I argue that better understanding of these diverse realms will strengthen the theory-building process. I argue that the boundaries between domains are where creativity flourishes and where advances are to be found. I examine how such boundary areas may function and identify some difficulties which may be encountered in bridging areas of expertise. I have based this paper on an invited closing address at the IMMS conference in January 2006. I have written from a personal perspective, drawing on my background in clinical practice (as a surgeon and a primary care physician), in education (as a general practitioner trainer and a developer of training programs) and in research (as an academic with a particular interest in surgical simulation). BACKGROUND The landscape of clinical practice is being radically altered by external and internal forces. Changes in established models of healthcare delivery are being driven by changing patterns of care (with increasing emphasis on targets and service outcomes) and reduction in working hours (both in Europe and the United States).1–3 Traditional service-based apprenticeship extending over many years is being supplanted by more focused, learner-centered programs aimed at achieving specific educational objectives in a much shorter time.4–10 The potential benefits of simulation are widely acknowledged, offering opportunities to practice repeatedly and in safety. Anesthesia-based team training and crisis resource management have led the move from task based practice to performing within authentic situations. Now patient-specific simulations are poised to create a whole new level of realism, using imaging and other data to provide authentic recreations of individual people. For many within healthcare, simulation is seen as a means of repeatedly practicing specific clinical tasks. Of course this is an important function, but it represents only a small part of simulation’s potential, and a task-focused philosophy can obscure the wider picture. If simulation is framed as a response to wider changes in the healthcare environment, a logical conclusion is that it should recreate as closely as possible the conditions of actual practice. These will include teamworking, leadership, crisis management, and many other elements. In this way, simulation can offer an alternative universe, where learners may safely experience issues which parallel those in real life. Seen from this viewpoint, simulation must provide not just a series of individual tasks, but rather a canvas upon which the elements of practice can be painted as required. Moreover, such environments should support that construction of professional identity which takes place within the clinical workplace through participation in communities of practice and of learning.11–13 In this sense, simulation is less of a physical reality than a conceptual space within which many activities can occur. To be effective, simulation must parallel its real world counterpart in a functional sense, even if it does not recreate reality in every detail. We must therefore examine the intersecting domains which relate to the various activities which simulation subsumes. These are illustrated by the issue of complexity. LEVELS OF COMPLEXITY Consider an apparently simple procedure such as closing a skin laceration with sutures. Simulation allows a learner to practice the technical aspects of this relatively straightforward task, repeatedly and safely. If these skills are to mean anything, however, they must be applied within a second level, that of clinical context. The clinician must relate to the patient before, during and after the technical procedure and, when the patient is conscious, while performing it. The clinician must take into account the patient’s ideas, concerns, and expectations, managing a holistic consultation at the same time as performing a procedure. In addition, each clinician must interact with other members of the healthcare team. For a novice, this integration of technical with nontechnical skills may be difficult enough even if the case is straightforward. If the patient is challenging (angry, upset, suffering from a disability or unable to speak the clinician’s language), or if there are problems with teamworking, the difficulties increase enormously. Yet it is the ability to perform in this wider and unpredictable context that characterizes the effective clinician. If the clinical task is more advanced (such as anesthesia and surgery), the potential for complexity increases enormously. Thirdly, there are the wider influences which bear on clinical practice, such as policy pressures, workforce design, economic imperatives, healthcare priorities, and the limitations or opportunities of funding. By shaping the care we provide, these exert a profound effect on the choices we make and the constraints under which we work, even if they are not directly involved in simulation-based training. So an awareness of such issues is crucial for effective simulation design, if it is to reflect the realities of our world and not simply create an oversimplified world which works within its own rules. Yet although there must obviously be a close concordance between simulation and its clinical counterpart, there are important differences too. In clinical practice, care of the patient is the overriding imperative. In simulation, although patient care must remain at center stage, the focus is on the learner. Moreover, simulation offers a kaleidoscope of shifting patterns made up of many disciplines. Simulators themselves form part of this space but do not constitute it wholly. When we move towards more authentic recreations of clinical situations, the need for integrating the elements of simulation becomes acute. An effective educational framework is essential to ensure that participants learn and (where appropriate) are assessed. Yet we have much to discover about teaching and learning within simulated environments. It is here that the need for a theory of simulation becomes increasingly compelling. Using the language of complexity theory, we can think of healthcare as a complex adaptive system.14,15 As with other such systems (such as the weather or the environment), there is no simple relationship between cause and effect. Accurate prediction of outcomes can be problematic. A major benefit of simulation is to expose learners to this very complexity, yet without the hazards of real life. Teaching, learning and clinical practice (each a complex system in itself) must therefore take place alongside one another within a simulated universe. REALISM A key issue is a simulation’s fitness for purpose, especially in relation to an overarching educational framework. For example, it is commonly held that the more realistic a simulation, the more effective it will be. Apart from its economic implications, this view privileges the position of complex technology within simulation. Although such technology is obviously essential in some instances (eg, training for procedures requiring advanced manipulative skills), too much emphasis on technology for its own sake may obscure important issues. Moreover, in a resource-limited environment there are opportunity costs in selecting particular elements of simulation at the expense of others. However, the relationship between realism and effectiveness is not a simple one, and surface realism may not always be necessary or even desirable. Moreover, what is perceived as realistic by one clinician may not be so for another. We have much to learn about the effect of experience on personal ways of seeing and of perceiving. It may be, for example, that minimal cues can stimulate a mental representation of clinical practice which is effective for some forms of training, such as urological endoscopy, without requiring expensive and elaborate simulators.16 On closer examination, therefore, fitness for purpose is a complex issue where firm theoretical foundations must underpin everyday judgements. Perhaps a more productive approach is to view realism as a negotiable currency which can be used flexibly in different settings. This requires a balance to be struck between the needs of learners and teachers and the resources that are available. In this way, we can keep sight of the overall aims of simulation rather than striving towards realism for its own sake. Again, a theory of simulation will give focus. BOUNDARY ZONES If we accept that simulation requires contact between disciplines, we must consider how such disciplines relate to one another, especially because no one practitioner will be expert in all the domains which contemporary simulation requires. For example, few clinicians have detailed knowledge of simulator programming and technical design, whereas nonclinical scientists may lack insight into the challenges of patient care and teamworking. It is at the edges of domains that most growth occurs. Of course there is much valuable work in the centers too, but by definition this takes place within an established field. Much of the impetus to change and grow comes from constructive friction between different domains and fields (for example, the combination of clinical imaging techniques with simulator technology to develop patient-specific simulations). It is here that cross fertilization of ideas takes place and that creative energy resides. Boundary zones—where the growing points of different fields intersect—are the most likely places to find these seminal events. This resonates with developments elsewhere in education, where pedagogical techniques that use technologies in constructive ways to teach content are being explored.17 This resonates with Kuhn’s distinction between normal science and scientific revolutions.18 Science, in Kuhn’s view, is not the steady, cumulative acquisition of knowledge that is portrayed in the textbooks. Rather, it is a series of peaceful interludes punctuated by intellectually violent revolutions in each of which one conceptual world view is replaced by another. Kuhn points out myriad examples of this process, from the discoveries of oxygen and x-rays to the convulsive paradigm shift of quantum mechanics. Simulation provides much scope for domains to intersect. Figure 1 is a list based on my personal experience and reading in my fields of research. For others the list may be different but the principles are the same. To illustrate this point I will use as an example the relationship between acting and clinical training, drawing on a scenario-based approach which my colleagues and I have developed for procedural skills.19–21 This example is intended to highlight areas of contact between 2 professions which function largely separately but where each can learn from the other.FIGURE 1.: Domains relevant to simulation. The following list is based on my own experience and is not intended to be exhaustive.Scenario-based assessment combines models or items of medical equipment with Simulated Patients (SPs; professional actors trained to play the part of real patients and then provide feedback), creating a realistic quasi-clinical environment where professional behaviors can be explored in addition to technical skills. In contrast to the isolated benchtop model, this kind of simulation appears to tap into a network of clinical responses activated by a realistic environment. This approach frames clinical procedures as “performance,” drawing heavily on the actors’ professional expertise and experience. From the actors’ point of view, key elements of effective performance include learning a part, managing props, remaining sensitive to their audience’s response and integrating all these elements seamlessly within a convincing performance which, if successful, hardly seems like a performance at all. Our experience has been that the actors’ contribution can far surpass the immediate requirement of creating a realistic encounter through mimicking a patient. A skilful SP performs at another level too, stepping out of role to provide feedback that is grounded in their authentic response to a quasi-clinical experience yet free from the power issues that can inhibit frank feedback between a sick patient and the clinician responsible for their care. At another level still, the professional expertise of the actor is itself a resource which, if skillfully exploited and suitably mediated, can be invaluable to the clinician. Simulation therefore offers opportunities for clinicians to “act” within a safe environment, focusing on performance skills which are commonly taken for granted or not recognized as legitimate components of expert clinical practice. All these are skills which a clinician needs as part of their own expert “performance” with each patient. Yet clinicians seldom see themselves as professional performers. To appreciate the artistry and expertise of the professional actor—the art which conceals art—we need insight into the process of acting. In many cases, this can be provided by the actors themselves, who can articulate their methods rather than simply performing.22 In this way, the learner gains a different level of perception and insight than simply “working on” the SP as a surrogate patient. This process is valuable in the other direction too, and SPs report that working with doctors and patients provides them with a different perspective which enriches their stage performances. If this open-minded engagement with experts from another profession is the case for acting, why should it not be so for the many other domains which bear upon simulation? For example, as clinicians we need an understanding of computer and materials technology, at least so that we can appreciate the possibilities and limitations of the field. Equally, as simulator designers we need an understanding of clinical practice. And such insight is essential in whichever areas we brush up against—not so that we can pretend to expertise in those fields, but so that we are aware of what they can offer us. TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION This process of constructive engagement can be easier said than done. If a wider view of simulation requires the integration of domains and effective collaboration at boundary areas, what obstacles might there be? Each of the domains in Figure 1 has its own traditions, its own literature, its own language, its own paradigms. When I was working towards a PhD (examining the application of an innovative approach to surgical skills training from an educational perspective), I initially encountered considerable difficulties in bridging the gap between my surgical background (with its heavy emphasis on a positivist scientific tradition and implicit assumptions about the existence of a single external reality) and the literature of education and the humanities (with its more contested views of truth). I grappled uncomfortably with an unfamiliar paradigm, and it was some time before I could engage effectively with these different domains and integrate their ideas with my own thinking. This was thrown into sharp focus when I came to combine quantitative and qualitative methodologies in my experimental design. From this experience I formulated the notion of total internal reflection as a metaphor for examining relationships between domains.23 Total internal reflection is an analogy from elementary physics and refers to the reflection of light from a surface without penetrating it. A goldfish inside a goldfish bowl would only be able to see within his own bowl and would be unaware of any world outside it. Indeed, he might be unaware that he was in a bowl at all. In my experience, a similar lack of awareness can affect those attempting to make contact with an unfamiliar domain. A creative rapprochement between different intellectual traditions is one simulation’s most attractive benefits. Yet we cannot assume that good will and enthusiasm are all that is required. The very richness and diversity of the fields can mask the effort required to understand where other contributors are coming from. Unless we recognize the dangers of total internal reflection, we may miss opportunities to capitalize on the creative possibilities which boundary areas present. Moreover, awareness of other domains and enthusiasm for their ideas is not enough. As scientists we need to maintain a criticality that assures our rigour and detachment if we are to avoid being swept along by fashion. CONCLUSION Simulation is an exciting area that offers enormous potential for developing innovative approaches to clinical education. Different groups will use it in different ways according to their needs: some with a narrow, task-based focus and other reaching out more widely. Perhaps one of simulation’s most attractive possibilities is the scope to draw creatively on other domains. However, in developing what simulation can offer we must remain critical, maintaining the rigour which defines us as scientists. If we are to draw on other domains yet still keep our sense of balance, we need to understand enough about these domains to assess critically what they can offer. This requires us to have sufficient knowledge to engage with them on their own terms. If we do not make this effort we risk becoming magpies, picking up glittering ideas but remaining ignorant of the philosophies which underpin them. The challenge to us in this evolving field is to reach out and explore other domains, building on the expertise which is out there. But in the process we must forge an identity of healthcare simulation with its own individuality. A “theory of simulation” is key to establishing a science which allows us to formulate and test hypotheses, engaging critically with an evidence base which transcends the accumulation of nuggets of knowledge. In this way, we will establish a creative, challenging yet mutually respectful alignment between our field and the sources of inspiration which must feed it. title: Switzerland in Europe. Continuity and Change in the Swiss Political Economy
abstract: Switzerland in Europe. Continuity and Change in the Swiss Political Economy Trampusch, Christine and Mach, André ( eds .) Abingdon : Routledge ( 2011 ), 244 p., ISBN 978-0-415-58051-9 The volume Switzerland in Europe edited by Christine Trampusch and André Mach is a salutary initiative. It provides the first comprehensive overview of the Swiss political economy. The editors crafted a volume that is resolutely comparative and international in outlook. Recent political-economic developments are assessed against the background of the experiences of other European countries, and major theories from political economy research are deployed to offer insights into the distinctive features of the Swiss political economy and the dynamics of continuity and change. The volume unquestionably fills an important void. It brings to the international, English-speaking audience a rich and authoritative account of the Swiss political economy. But it also addresses a domestic readership, students of Swiss politics. It is a suitable manual for teaching Swiss political economy – I have not hesitated an instant to adopt it as a textbook in my own teaching on the subject. The editors brought together a balanced mix of established scholars, promising young academics, and creative PhD students to produce 13 chapters organized in four parts. After a brief first chapter that serves as a general introduction to the volume (André Mach and Christine Trampusch), part one sets the stage by providing elements of context. Chapter two by the same authors discusses the placement of Switzerland in the available typologies of comparative research and outlines the distinctive features of the Swiss political economy. It also provides background information about the 1990s – a period of protracted economic crisis – which is conjectured (and later confirmed) to be a turning point in Switzerland’s post-war political-economic development. Chapter three (Fritz Sager and Christine Zollinger) and four (Wolf Linder) offer an overview of domestic and external factors, respectively, focusing on formal political institutions of the Swiss political system and Switzerland’s relationship with the European Union (it is argued that, for Switzerland, globalization has taken the form of Europeanization). Parts two through four go to the core of the matter by addressing different domains and policy fields of the political economy. Part two on economic actors comprises two superb chapters on organized capital (Pierre Eichenberger and André Mach) and organized labor and industrial relations (Daniel Oesch). Part three, entitled “major socio-economic institutions”, covers corporate governance (Gerhard Schnyder and Frédéric Widmer), labor market (Patrick Emmenegger), and skill formation (Linda Rohrer and Christine Trampusch). Part four, dealing with economic and social policies, includes chapters on corporatism (Klaus Armingeon), the welfare state (Giuliano Bonoli and Silja Häusermann) and regulatory policies (Martino Maggetti, Alexandre Afonso and Marie-Christine Fontana). A final chapter by Yannis Papadopoulos wraps up the findings and addresses the question how much and in what ways has Switzerland changed. Overall, the contributors by and large share a historical-institutionalist perspective (with the “varieties of capitalism” approach featuring most prominently) and draw heavily on case studies, thereby forming a coherent whole both theoretically and methodologically. What are the main take-home points? (It is not possible within the scope of this review to do justice to the rich and nuanced analysis presented in each chapter.) I see mainly three. First, building on the observation that the Swiss political economy sits uneasily in the seminal typologies of comparative political economy (i.e., Katzenstein’s small corporatist states; Esping-Andersen’s welfare state regimes; Hall and Soskice’s varieties of capitalism), Mach and Trampusch (chapter two) take on the ambitious task of conceptual clarification. The authors endorse the “Sonderfall Schweiz” thesis in that Switzerland represents a hybrid case whatever the typology one chooses. More importantly, they suggest three building blocks of the Swiss political-economic order: 1) constrained policy capacity of the central state; 2) strong tradition of self-regulation by economic associations; and 3) dominance of right-wing parties and business associations (pp. 14–19). Such a depiction dovetails with the tradition in political economy associated with Katzenstein (1985) that focuses on the role and structure of the state in political-economic development (rather than with the approach focusing on the coordination capacity of firms). While the authors acknowledge that Katzenstein’s analysis of small states in world markets and his differentiation between liberal and social corporatism is the most suited to grasp the Swiss case (p. 12), they do not address in what ways their own categories differ from those underpinning liberal corporatism. What strikes me are similarities rather than differences. Negotiated development involving interest groups and the state bureaucracy under the wings of an enabling state seem to largely overlap with the notions of limited state capacity and self-regulation by economic actors. And the upper hand of organized business in liberal corporatism (resulting in private compensation) captures the idea of the dominance of the right-wing parties and business associations. Moreover, a political economy perspective typically entails a shift away from voters and parties to producer groups, and so one may question the decision to include partisan considerations in the core features defining a political economy. More generally, the criticisms addressed to Katzenstein’s work from the Swiss vantage point, which would help justify why one parts way with his conceptualization, are passed under silence. Second, with regard to the degree of change, there is considerable agreement among the authors that change over the past two decades has been far-reaching. Change is particularly visible in the domains of social policy (pensions, unemployment and invalidity insurance), industrial relations (decentralization of collective bargaining, slowing down/stagnation of working time reduction, facilitation of extension clauses), vocational training (increasing importance of both general and firm-specific firms), corporate governance (emergence of an active market for corporate control), as well as the organization of business associations (growing heterogeneity and divisions) and trade unions (mergers). Scholars of comparative politics should take notice because Switzerland is traditionally considered a “least likely” case given its political institutions that generate a status quo bias in decision making. Third, in terms of the nature of the change, the overall trend is one towards more liberalism (p. 234). The major exception is the “flanking measures” negotiated within the framework of the bilateral agreements between the EU and Switzerland regarding the free movement of persons, which re-regulated the labor market by facilitating the extension of collective agreements and the monitoring of social dumping practices (see chapter by Oesch). One is tempted to conclude that some form of the “compensation hypothesis” (Katzenstein 1985) is alive. And the trajectory in social policy needs to be qualified, as Switzerland changed from a liberal to a liberal-conservative welfare state as a result of a catching-up process over the past three decades (see chapters by Armingeon and by Bonoli and Häusermann). Despite its innovative character, the volume could benefit from a broader coverage of issues. Given how much attention rising inequality has recently received in research and politics, it is regrettable that the book glosses over taxation and more generally (the politics of) redistribution. One would expect growing income inequalities as a result of increased liberalism in the context of economic globalization and skilled-biased technological change (both inequality-increasing factors). After all, inequality is on the rise in most OECD countries (OECD 2011). Surprisingly, Switzerland is among the few outliers (together with France and Belgium). The contrast with traditionally low-inequality Germany, with whom it shares many similar economic, social and cultural characteristics, is striking. Whereas in Germany inequality increased markedly in recent years (OECD 2011: 24), in Switzerland inequality in market income remained steady and inequality in disposable income (i.e., post-tax, post-transfer) decreased slightly between the early 1980s and the mid-2000s. 1 What is more, as of the late 2000s, inequality of disposable income among working-age persons was lower in Switzerland than in Germany (OECD 2011: 36). Policy choices appear to go a long way in explaining these differences. Whereas Germany significantly loosened employment protection legislation for workers with temporary contracts and increased it for regular workers in the three decades between 1985 and 2007, Switzerland did neither (see chapter by Emmenegger). More importantly, government redistribution through tax/transfers became less efficient in Germany, driven mainly by cuts in the generosity of unemployment benefits introduced in the mid-2000s, but actually increased in Switzerland where increases in social transfers between the early 1990s and the mid-2000s more than offset reductions in personal income tax (OECD 2011: 37). Two other prominent topics shine by their absence. First, the rise of non-standard employment contracts (e.g., part-time, temporary contracts) and the associated labor market dualization. The stability in employment protection legislation does not preclude the shares of the labor force that fall under one or the other type of employment regulation to change. Second, macro-economic management, in particular fiscal and monetary policies. This is of course particularly relevant in the context of the government responses to the Great Recession of 2008–2009 which concentrated heavily on fiscal stimulus and monetary easing (i.e., the sudden and surprising revival of Keynesianism). As Switzerland appears to have weathered the storm better than others, an analysis of the contribution of fiscal and monetary policy to crisis management and/or to economic performance in general would be desirable. Does the book pass the test of being a valuable textbook for teaching Swiss political economy? I carried out a first test by asking my students to assess the volume on a number of dimensions using a response scale ranging from 0 (fully disagree) to 10 (fully agree). These are the results (N = 10). Does the manual provide a systematic introduction to the Swiss political economy? The average response is 8.3 (stan. dev. is .8). Does it provide insights into important theories in comparative political economy? This question yields a mean of 7.8 (stan. dev. 1.2). Taken together, these results suggest that the volume is successful in achieving its own stated goals. When asked about the overall satisfaction with the manual, the mean response score drops to 6.6 (stan. dev. .8). One may speculate a bit why this is so. Although all chapters are highly informative, there is some variation in quality. Also, assigning journal articles alongside book chapters is essential as the former offer stronger causal claims and empirical tests. Regarding causality, Papadopoulos concludes that “a systematic scrutiny of causal mechanisms leading to change – that may differ, at least in part, depending on the objects of change – is still outstanding” (p. 235). While reading the book does indeed leave us with this impression, it is also true that the more demanding task of systematic causal inference has been accomplished to a considerable extent elsewhere in the works by these authors. Yet opening up the circle beyond contributors writing within the comparative, historical-institutionalist perspective could yield novel insights into the rapidly changing Swiss political economy.

title: Medical work hours: time for a Maggie's Law for doctoring?
abstract: In June 2003, the New Jersey state legislature passed ‘Maggie's Law’ establishing that causing vehicular homicide without having sleep for a period in excess of 24 consecutive hours is a criminal offence1. This law was passed after intensive lobbying by the family of 20-year-old college student Maggie McDonnell, who was killed when a driver crossed three lanes of highway traffic and hit her car head-on. The male driver admitted he had been awake for 30 h before the accident, but due to a lack of legal precedent, with driving without sleep not being considered a ‘crime’, he received only a suspended jail sentence and $200 fine. In the UK, a driver who was alleged to have fallen asleep at the wheel after a night without sleep ran onto a main train track causing the Selby train disaster, and was recently jailed for 5 years2. Increasingly, society and its legal systems are recognizing that, for most people, falling asleep behind the wheel is foreseeable, avoidable and an act of criminal recklessness. Although falling asleep behind the wheel is a well-recognized outcome of sleep deprivation, what about falling asleep behind the scalpel or advancing central line? It has been long known that there is an increased incidence of medical errors following sleep deprivation. In 1971, researchers at Columbia University Medical School reported that interns made twice as many electrocardiogram reading errors after working extended shifts (24 h or more) compared with after a normal nights’ sleep3. Subsequent literature reviews highlighted the dangers of extended medical work hours, but studies were often limited by either imprecise measurement of sleep hours or questionable surrogates for work performance4, 5. Further, investigations showing increased errors on realistic surgical or anaesthetic simulators, following conditions of on-call or sleep loss, have provided strongly suggestive data that lack of sleep seriously impairs work performance by medical staff4-8. These data and public concerns over resident working hours resulted in the US Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) introducing new work-hour rules for residency programmes effective from July 20039. The changes included limiting weekly work hours to a maximum of 80 duty hours per week (or 88 h/week in case of special education needs) averaged over 4 weeks and single duty periods limited to no more than 24 h (although residents may remain on duty for 6 additional hours for continuity of care or education). To many in Australia, these ‘changes’ may seem inappropriately loose regulatory steps considering the resident medical officer rosters currently existing in our teaching hospitals. However, Australian Institute of Health and Welfare Medical Work Force data indicate that up to 15% of medical practitioners work over 80 h per week suggesting that we do not exist in a safe work hours paradise. Interestingly, a number of US commentators and reviewers has questioned the ACGME limits on working hours as having been instituted without objective evidence of their efficacy in improving patient safety10, 11. Moreover, others raise concerns about the impact of reduced working hours on continuity of care and education12. Further data strengthening these concerns were recently provided by two landmark articles published in the October 28, 2004 edition of the New England Journal of Medicine13, 14. The articles describe different aspects of the Intern Sleep and Patient Safety Study undertaken by the Division of Sleep Medicine at Harvard University Medical School. The crossover study design involved a prospective randomised trial comparing two intern shift schedules in an intensive care unit (ICU) –‘traditional schedule’ with extended (24 h or more from morning rounds on day 2 to afternoon rounds on day 3) work shifts every other shift (every third night on duty) and an ‘intervention’ schedule that eliminated extended shifts by splitting them into two halves worked on separate days. In addition, during the intervention arm, interns were advised to take a nap on their free afternoon prior to their night shift. This was unavailable during the traditional arm as the interns were working a continuous shift at this time. Sleep and attentional failures were monitored by self-report, observation and objective monitoring with continuous electroencephalogram and electro-oculogram measures. Medical errors were measured by a complex system of observation and chart reviews and categorized by blinded observers. The Harvard study provided wide-ranging new data that over time will impact on future medical work-hours policy. The shift intervention in the ICU setting resulted in 20 less work hours per week (on the ‘traditional’ roster, interns worked an average of 85 h per week), more objectively monitored and subjectively reported sleep (6 h/week), more sleep in the 24 h preceding each working shift and less than half the rate of attentional failures/‘microsleeps’ on night duty. Importantly, this translated to a significantly lower medical error rate than on the traditional shift. During the traditional roster, interns made 36% more serious medical errors (136 vs 100 per 1000 patient/days) and 57% more serious errors that were not intercepted by other staff. The serious errors that were more frequent on the traditional roster were medication errors and diagnostic errors (5.6 times higher, 18.6 vs 3.3 per 1000 patient days). There was no difference in procedural errors, but these occurred relatively infrequently. In his editorial on these publications, Jeffrey Drazen, the New England Journal of Medicine editor, commented ‘these two articles ... have convinced me that we need to replace the traditional system with one in which the responsibilities for patient care are shared by a team and that allows physicians to get more sleep’15. The consequences of sleep loss are becoming more well known16. Recent data have highlighted that chronic sleep restriction typified by multiple 24-h periods with shortened sleep are associated with marked decrements in performance without matching subjective recognition of these deficits17, 18. Sleep loss may also have serious metabolic and other physiological consequences19. Health workers are also vulnerable to other pressures on their time available for sleep, including leisure activities, ‘moonlighting’ in second jobs or extra shifts, young children and sleep or other medical disorders. There is also heightened awareness of inter-individual vulnerability in the neurobehavioural effects of sleep loss20. Some individuals are particularly vulnerable to restricted sleep hours or have difficulty sleeping during the day. With the added circadian disruption of rotating shift work, individuals may develop chronic sleep problems and difficulty maintaining sufficient alertness at work. In a more extreme form, this may include the clinical diagnosis of ‘shift work sleep disorder’21. We currently do not have systems that can objectively and accurately detect vulnerable health-care workers with problems maintaining alertness. How many of us laugh when colleagues fall asleep in clinical meetings rather than ask if this individual is safe to diagnose illnesses or cut open an abdomen? The other frightening side is evidence of the high incidence of fall-asleep accidents in medical officers driving home from work22. The days of old-world medical stoicism and ‘in my day’ anecdotes have been met head-on by this Harvard study. Can surgeons take comfort from the lack of difference in rates of procedural errors between the two arms of this study? Probably not – the study was not powered to detect differences in procedural errors which are relatively infrequent events compared to medication errors. Surgical simulators suggest dexterity is impaired by sleep loss. Moreover, as one Lancet letter writer summed up – who would give informed consent in a trial comparing outcomes of operations by sleep deprived versus rested surgeons? The arguments that long work hours are needed for education and training should be tempered by the impact of sleep loss on learning itself23, 24. In the US, Johns Hopkins University had its accreditation for residency training programmes withdrawn due to violation of work-hour rules (http:www.ama-assn.orgamednews20030915prsc0915.htm). An interesting side-issue of the Harvard study was clear evidence of breaches in work-hour rules during the traditional shift arm, no doubt necessitating some rapid roster changes pre-publication13, 14. There are medico-legal implications of this information on the risks of sleep loss in interns in Australia and New Zealand (http:www.amaq.com.auindex.php?action view&view1393&pid1355). Just as society is tiring of dangerous drivers escaping punishment due to ‘fall asleep’ defences, there is evidence of a harsher legal climate for doctors who continue to work despite sleep loss. Moreover, under new occupational health law initiatives in Australia, there is a chain of responsibility for unsafe work systems that potentially means administrators, staff specialists and even visiting consultants can be held responsible for errors caused by their junior staff or even motor vehicle accidents driving home from work22. Senior staff need to look at their own work hours and sleep health. The highly vulnerable super-specialty registrar who is seemingly permanently ‘on-call’ needs to have their work hours closely monitored with consultants stepping into this roster if sleep loss accumulates to a dangerous level. Otherwise it will be only a matter of time before there will be a Maggie's Law for doctoring. Received 10 January 2005; accepted 10 January 2005.

title: Custom-Made Titanium Mesh for Maxillary Bone Augmentation With Immediate Implants and Delayed Loading
abstract: During the past 30 years, guided bone regeneration (GBR) has been successfully performed to treat fenestration, alveolar dehiscence, extraction sockets, and various alveolar ridge deficiencies. Providing spaces using barrier membranes combined with bone graft materials contributes to the best long-term stability of the newly augmented site. As a result of the ongoing research on GBR, many methods to increase bone volume have improved, various materials have been studied to induce new tissue growth, and numerous barrier membranes have been developed for different clinical situations.1Titanium-reinforced polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) membranes stabilized with pins and screws are often considered the most predictable technique for increasing bone volume in larger alveolar ridge deficiencies prior to or during implant surgery.1 Titanium mesh shows similar results for alveolar ridge deficiencies because of its excellent mechanical properties for the stabilization of bone grafts such as high strength, low density, plasticity, and low weight. In addition, its rigidity provides space maintenance and prevents contour collapse, its smooth surface decreases bacterial contamination, and its stability wards off graft displacement.2 New advances in tissue engineering technology are significantly improving clinical performance with this type of barrier. The use of computer-aided design (CAD) and computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) in health care fields such as dentistry has allowed manufacturers to go beyond previous limits and obtain various morphologies from different devices with high accuracy, thereby increasing treatment opportunities in some clinical situations.2,3 This technology combined with a selective laser melting machine can provide porous titanium structures with complex geometries that control the internal architecture. The main advantage of this technology is that it can produce custom-made devices for bone augmentation that are individually suited for patients requiring implant rehabilitation.4We investigated the basic principles of digital workflow and the surgical steps of a novel type of custom-made titanium mesh (Ti-mesh), validated this surgical approach for bone augmentation in an edentulous atrophic maxilla, and analyzed the stability of the augmented bone after 1 year of follow-up.A 56-year-old male patient presented with a completely edentulous maxilla (Figure 1) and no general contraindications to oral surgery; he asked for fixed rehabilitation.Preoperative orthopantography (Figure 2) showed a sufficient bone height to place standard implants, but computerized tomography (CT) highlighted insufficient bone width due to moderate horizontal bone resorption in the anterior maxilla. Because of the observed implant fenestration and dehiscence in the anterior maxilla (Figure 3), a horizontal bone augmentation procedure was planned, to be conducted simultaneously with implant placement.A customized Ti-mesh was designed based on CT data using CAD-CAM software (BTK Opera Software, BTK, Biotec srl, Polovaro di Dueville, Italy). The digital workflow included the following steps: DICOM files of CT were used to create a 3-dimensional (3D) model of the maxilla (Figure 4), bone volume was horizontally increased and shaped to reconstruct the atrophic maxilla, a 0.3-mm layer was placed on the augmented maxilla to cover the whole bone volume (Figure 5), and finally, a virtual mesh was created from the layer, choosing structure, weave, fixation holes, and margins that fit perfectly over the borders of the bone defect (Figures 6 and 7). After software elaboration, the data were used to realize the customized Ti-mesh using a laser-sintering 3D printer (ProX-DMP100, 3D System, Rock Hill, SC).After local anesthesia, a mid-crestal incision was made from one maxillary tuberosity to the other, and a full-thickness flap was raised to expose the maxillary jaw. After preparation of implant sites, four tapered double-lead thread implants (NobelActive, Nobel Biocare, Zurich, Switzerland) were placed in the maxilla (Figure 8) and in the mandibular bone. A 50:50 mixture of autologous bone and xenograft (Zcore Porcine Xenograft, Osteogenics, Lubbock, Tex) was enhanced with plasma rich in growth factors (PRGF; PRGF-Endoret; BTI Biotechnology Institute, Vitoria, Spain) and used as grafting material to fill the Ti-mesh that was fixed to the anterior maxilla using titanium mini-screws (Pro-fix System, Osteogenics). Then, PRGF membranes were applied over the Ti-mesh to facilitate the healing of soft tissue. After buccal flap passivation was obtained with periosteal incisions, a tension-free primary closure with 5-0 PTFE sutures was completed (Cytoplast, Osteogenics; Figure 9). After 6 months of submerged healing, reopening surgery for Ti-mesh removal and implant exposure was performed (Figure 10). After 3 months, the definitive full-arch fixed prosthesis was delivered to rehabilitate the esthetics and function of the patient (Figure 11).As shown in this case report, the digital workflow is a safe and predictable procedure because of the quality of CT image acquisition and the printing precision of Ti-mesh.3,4 A customized Ti-mesh can have many advantages. This fabrication process offers a bended grid with neat and clean margins, without irregularities and imprecision that may harm soft tissue. The precise adaptation of the mesh to regenerative material and native bone may help reduce micro-movements. In addition, the fabrication process eliminates the need to manually adapt the mesh to the patient, which significantly reduces the working time, open flap period, risk of contamination, and, consequently, postoperative infections.2–4The risk of early or late exposure is the main drawback of Ti-mesh and seems to correlate with wearing a mobile prosthesis and/or inadequate modeling of the mesh.4,5 Accurate digital planning and a careful prosthetic protocol during the first 3 months of healing seem to be key factors for avoiding biological complications (ie, exposure of Ti-mesh). After removal of the Ti-mesh, a layer of connective tissue covering the newly formed bone, the so-called “pseudo-periosteum,” was observed. This is indicative of a lack of bone regeneration due to infiltration of connective tissue across the mesh holes and does not allow for verification of bone density and features of augmented bone but seems to protect the bone in case of exposure.After 1 year of loading (Figures 12 and 13), CT was useful for evaluating the structure and stability of the augmented bone. All implants were entirely surrounded by bone tissue on the buccal side, and there was a new cortical layer due to reorganization and remineralization of newly formed bone; the old cortical layer was still detectable in the scans (Figure 14). The rationale to place implants simultaneously with horizontal bone augmentation was based on a reference point to verify the reduction of augmented bone over time.In summary, the advantages of 3D designing and printing a customized Ti-mesh are the high stability of the regenerative material, neat margins and no sharp edges, only 2 or 3 vestibular pins needed to fix the mesh, working time reduction, infection risk reduction, and previsualization of the result.With proper patient selection, careful diagnostic procedures, and advanced surgical skills, this technique could become a valid alternative to standard Ti-mesh in the edentulous atrophic maxilla. The predictability of this technique permits simultaneous implant placement without compromising bone regeneration over the implants in cases of fenestration or dehiscence.Within the limit of a case report, immediate maxillary implant insertion with simultaneous horizontal bone augmentation with customized CAD/CAM Ti-mesh is a promising technique. Comparative studies with longer follow-up and a larger population are required to validate this simplified approach.The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

title: Labour’s 2019 Campaign: A Defeat of Epic Proportions
abstract: When the Prime Minister Boris Johnson called an early election, few Labour candidates were expecting a victory or even a repeat of the better than expected results obtained in the 2017 general election. Equally few, however, were prepared for the party to suffer such a comprehensively devastating defeat. Yet Labour obtained its worst election result since 1935, attracting less than one-third of the votes cast and electing only 202 MPs. Crucially, Labour lost 61 seats (and won one), many in traditional heartlands in northern England and in the Midlands, but the party also lost a sizeable number of seats in Scotland and Wales. Unsurprisingly, as soon as the electoral results arrived, the blame game began. For many observers and Labour candidates, the leader of the party, Jeremy Corbyn, was the main cause of Labour’s defeat. After all, he agreed to hold an election at the worst possible time, led a disorganised campaign and was extremely unpopular with voters. ‘Corbynistas’, on the other hand, blamed Labour’s pro-European faction, which forced the party to adopt a new policy on Brexit which, in their view explains the loss of dozens of seats in the North of England and Midlands. Doubtless, these factors contributed to Labour’s devastating defeat; however, other long-term factors, such as a decade of turbulent politics, structural changes to politics and the emergence of new cleavages contributed to Labour’s fourth consecutive defeat since 2010. This chapter will explain the short-term and long-term factors that led to Labour’s defeat but it will start by contextualising Labour’s state of readiness for the election and analysing Labour’s 2019 electoral campaign. Labour’s better-than-expected results at the 2017 general election offered some breathing space to its leader. The planned plots to oust Corbyn were put on hold and so were the ‘Save Jeremy’ campaign devised by his team (Shipman, 2018, p. 448). Moreover, as the new intake of MPs was supportive of his agenda, Corbyn was able to tighten his control over the party. Over time, the Left became the dominant voice of the party’s National Executive Committee and main decision-making structures of the party. When the party met in Brighton for its annual conference in September 2017 the mood was, to use the words of Corbyn’s former adviser Andrew Fisher, ‘hubristic’ (Evening Standard, 2020). Reflecting that mood, Corbyn told delegates that Labour had become ‘a government-in-waiting’ that was ‘setting the agenda and winning the arguments for a new common sense about the direction our country should take’ (Corbyn, 2019c). The Shadow Chancellor, John McDonnell, responded to Corbyn’s call by turbo-charging the party’s policy-making engine and by focussing on improving the party’s economic credibility. He led workshops on alternative forms of ownerships, listened to economists on productivity and launched several ‘tea-charm offensives’ to the City of London and to Britain’s boardrooms in the hope of reassuring them that business was ‘better off with Labour’. But McDonnell’s efforts to turn Labour into a credible government in waiting were undermined by two major crises which paralysed the party for the best part of the two years that preceded the 2019 election. The first one was Corbyn’s failure to tackle decisively anti-semitic behaviour within the party; the second was his inability to develop a coherent approach to Brexit, the most important question facing the country at the time. The crisis of anti-Semitism emerged soon after Corbyn’s election as Labour leader in 2015 but it had acquired dramatic proportions by the summer of 2018. The party tried slowly, albeit with little resolve, to address the issue by adopting new internal rules to discipline members found guilty of anti-semitic behaviour. But those efforts backfired when, in March 2018, Jeremy Corbyn expressed his opposition to the defacing of an anti-semitic mural. The backbencher Luciana Berger questioned the leader’s office about Corbyn’s apparent endorsement of the mural. Corbyn’s office backtracked immediately and apologised but this reaction was deemed inadequate by Berger and other MPs. Even McDonnell and Momentum condemned Corbyn’s office for Labour’s failure to deal with anti-semitic behaviour in a decisive manner (Kogan, 2019, pp. 349–351). The mural incident was not the final one in the party’s anti-Semitism crisis. In the summer of 2018, Labour’s internal debate about the adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) definition of anti-semitism into the party’s code showed that Corbyn had not yet tackled the problem. The NEC’s proposed amendments to the definition were challenged by several frontbenchers who wanted Labour to adopt the full IHRA definition and by 68 British Rabbis, who published a letter in the Guardian (2018) condemning the party’s new code. Needless to say, the media coverage of the controversy did Labour no favours. This was a wound that continued to bleed. Another key moment in Labour’s anti-Semitism crisis emerged in February 2019, when Luciana Berger, together with seven other Labour backbenchers, defected from the party claiming institutional anti-Semitism. Labour’s anti-Semitism crisis escalated further when three months later, the Equality and Human Rights Commission launched an investigation into Labour’s anti-semitic behaviour. The extent of the party’s anti-semitic crisis was highlighted by the decision of the Jewish Labour Movement to refuse to campaign for the party at the 2019 election, quickly followed by the recommendation by the Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis to his congregants to vote for whichever party that is more likely to defeat Labour. Following this, Labour’s reputation as an anti-racist party was in tatters. The second problem that undermined Labour’s popularity was Brexit. The party’s 2017 manifesto accepted the results of the referendum on membership of the European Union (EU) as well as the end of free movement, while making some positive noises about a softer Brexit and the benefits of immigration (Labour Party, 2017). This ambivalent position was electorally astute (Mellon et al., 2018, p. 735), but following the general election, Corbyn was under pressure to adopt a more pro-European stance. Confronted with a divided parliamentary party on the most important issue of the day, Corbyn’s approach to Brexit was marked by obfuscation in the period between the two general elections. The party’s Shadow Brexit Secretary, Keir Starmer, told Labour’s 2018 conference in Liverpool that ‘nobody is ruling out Remain as an option’ in a second referendum. Corbyn appeared less enthused by such a move. It took months of campaigning by pro-European groups and trade unions, and the disastrous results of the European Parliament elections in June 2019, for Labour to adopt a clearer policy on Brexit. Finally, at the party’s 2019 annual conference, Corbyn announced that a Labour government would first negotiate a new withdrawal agreement with Brussels and then it would subject that deal to a new referendum where voters would also be given the option to vote to remain in the EU. But to the surprise of many, the Labour leader announced that he would remain neutral on the question and would implement the will of the people. Labour’s new Brexit policy, which reflected the views of the majority of Labour members (Bale et al., 2020, p. 70; Fieldhouse, 2019), was greeted with relief by activists who had been campaigning for the last two years for a new referendum on EU membership. However, Labour’s new position was announced just a few weeks before the general election and meant that the party had little time to explain it to voters. As a result, many candidates feared the worst. For candidates who represented Leave seats, it was clear that their voters would react angrily at the party’s blatant disrespect for the results of the 2016 referendum on EU membership (Cruddas, 2019). Others feared that Corbyn’s neutrality on the issue made him look indecisive and opportunistic. The party’s handling of these crises undermined Labour’s popularity, even among ‘Corbynistas’. The infectious enthusiasm of the youngsters who chanted ‘Oh, Jeremy Corbyn!’ at music festivals in 2017 waned as a result of the party’s inability to discipline anti-semitic behaviour, ambivalence over Brexit and resistance to democratising its policy-making structures. Indeed, as the Leader of the Opposition’s Office tightened its grip over the party’s policy-making machine, disillusion grew amongst activists. That disillusion was well captured by the convener of the left-wing grassroot movement Compass, Neal Lawson, who remarked that the ‘Labour leader’s office today is at least as powerful, and unaccountable, as it was under Blair and Brown. Whatever else it is, this is not bottom-up democracy’ (2019, p. 180). In a similar vein, Jeremy Gilbert, an academic who supported Corbyn, admitted that the leader’s office was ‘acquiring a reputation for secrecy, authoritarianism and narrow-mindedness that may have well been an inevitable product of seeking success within the Westminster system, but which threatens to demoralise the membership base’ (2019, p. 87). This account was confirmed by Andrew Fisher’s letter of resignation from the party, in which he accused the leader’s office of a ‘lack of professionalism, competence and human decency’ (quoted by Line and Bloom, 2019). title: A European Revival of Liberation Theology
abstract: What should Christianity be saying about global capitalism? The World Council of Churches, the World Alliance of Reformed Churches, and the Lutheran World Federation have begun a significant exploration of that question.It’s a discussion I hope you will bring into the churches of North America. The conversation doesn’t have to be limited to Christianity, either. What should Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, and Buddhism be saying about global capitalism? It’s a debate to bring into your synagogues, mosques, ashrams, and schools of theology and divinity, and into local secular communities as well, since the issues bear on the entire human race and the survival of the planet. After you develop a perspective on capitalism within your own religious group, you can then—as a community—share your views in the international debate now taking place. The global religious community could play an important role in challenging the growing materialism and selfishness that have characterized the growth of a global capitalist worldview.Not surprisingly, the process of creating a joint statement has sparked a rather striking debate among Christians about how explicitly we ought to challenge global capitalism. A group of us European theologians have put forward what we believe to be a rather strong statement of a Christian perspective—one that goes much further than many of our fellow Christians in the Northern hemisphere would choose. The perspective we articulate in “Life in Just Peace,” the joint statement reprinted below, better reflects the views of many Christians in the Southern hemisphere. To speak to some of the concerns that our visionary statement commonly raises among skeptics from the global North, I have constructed a response to an imagined criticism from a North American pastor (see page 78) that channels the type of energy and analysis more common among Christians from the global South.A joint statement by a group of twenty-six European initiatives and networks, including Kairos Europe, Pax Christi (German section), INKOTA, Christians for a Just Economic System, Pleading for an Ecumenical Future, Winds from the South, and several regional ecumenical grassroots networks, working together in the “German Ecumenical Network” in preparation for the May 2011 International Ecumenical Peace Convocation in Kingston, Jamaica.Humanity and the earth are undergoing a unique crisis. Above all, this is manifested in the form of the financial and economic crisis, the food crisis, the social crisis (the growing gap between those who are becoming poorer and those becoming richer), the energy crisis, the climate crisis, the crisis of the extinction of species and the crisis of increasing violence at all levels—from the family and schools to imperialist wars. The causes of these crises are clearly related to the dominant civilization, which from the “West” has conquered the entire globe in the areas of economics, politics, ideology, and the understanding of what it means to be human. This crisis is threatening life itself. As we see it, just peace must therefore be understood as leading toward a new culture of life at all levels—from institutional to spiritual life.The necessary turnaround toward a life in just peace includes at least three dimensions:A spiritual vision of a new, emerging culture of life based on faith or a humanist motivation.The fundamental rejection of the dominant economic, political, violence-producing culture and world order for the sake of the integrity of faith and the very being of the church.Short-, medium-, and long-term steps toward realizing this vision.We therefore present the following declaration, which is based on the biblical message and affirms decisions by the assemblies of ecumenical organizations, inviting all churches, congregations, and Christians to embrace it and to publicly advocate for the implementation of its demands.1. Which god shall rule?We believe that God created the whole universe in love, inviting all people to cooperate with God’s ongoing creative work in mutual solidarity and respect for God’s gifts. “The earth is the Lord’s and all that is in it” (Ps. 24:1). With faith in God’s Trinitarian dynamic we confess with all Christians the sociality of God as the source of the unity of all creatures.Therefore, we reject the current world economic order imposed by global neoliberal capitalism—using both structural and direct violence. We reject every claim to an economic, political, and military empire that attempts to subvert God’s order of life and whose actions stand in contrast to God’s love and justice. We reject an economic system and way of life that exploits nature and propagates unlimited growth so that the conditions of life for future generations are forcibly destroyed and the survival chances of the entire earth are threatened.The power of God’s Spirit frees us as individuals and churches to resist the ruling political-economic-cultural system and to work for crucially necessary alternatives.2. God’s good gifts for all should not be privatized by force.We believe that God is a God of life and desires the fullness of life for all creatures. “I came that they might have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10).Therefore we reject a policy that through the privatization of collective and common goods produces wealth for the capital owners but scarcity and poverty for the vast majority of the world’s population—the worst kind of violence (Gandhi)—and which exploits and even destroys nature. With particular emphasis we reject the patenting of seeds and of medicines that are necessary to meet people’s basic needs. We say no to the privatization of genes as well as acts of biopiracy; no to the privatization of water and other gifts of nature; no to the privatization of services of general interest such as energy, transportation, health, education; also no to the destruction of solidarity-based social insurance systems through privatization; no to their submission to profit-oriented insurance companies and at the same time to speculative finance markets. All of this is structural violence at the service of the rich. But especially we reject the direct violence of a policy that wages wars to realize these private interests and wastes immeasurable resources on armaments.The power of God’s Spirit frees us as individuals and churches to work for the democratizing of the economy and the solidarity-based social systems toward serving life, among ourselves and in society, so that all might have enough, so that neither hardship nor excessive consumption prevails and that the earth can remain intact for future generations. Economic systems should be for the common use and not for the expansion of capital. For this reason goods and services for basic needs as well as global common goods must be publically run for mutual benefit, so that in accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights all governments recognize their responsibility for the welfare of their citizens. We pledge to struggle for an order at all levels, in which economics and politics are put at the service of life for all and thereby overcome the fundamental causes of violence.3. God’s good earth should not be destroyed by greed.We believe that God entrusted human beings with a rich and beautiful earth. “The Lord took the human beings and put them in the Garden of Eden to till it and keep it” (Gen. 2:15).Therefore, we reject an economic and social order that converts God’s gifts into commodities and in so doing increasingly destroys them. We especially call on Christians, congregations, and churches in the industrialized countries to recognize their enormous ecological debts, particularly their destructive climate debts, toward people who have been living in impoverished regions for the past five hundred years, and at least to offer symbolic compensation, to radically reduce their harmful greenhouse emissions, and to oblige their governments to pass national and international laws to keep global warming under two degrees and to stop the extermination of species.The power of God’s Spirit frees us as individuals and churches to set an example and reduce our consumption of energy and the environment as well as to force our governments to establish binding rules for reduction under international law (allowing for transitional arrangements for newly industrialized and developing countries). All in all, we will work for a cyclical economy that makes the gifts of nature available for just and sustainable use.4. God liberates working people from violent exploitation.We believe that God intends human labor to become participation in God’s creative power and as a means for self-sufficiency in human societies, without exploiting working men and women. “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other Gods before me” (Gen. 20:2).Therefore, we reject an economic order in which working people, especially women, are (structurally or directly) violently exploited and driven into unemployment. We reject governments that tax workers more and more but levy less and less taxes on capital gains from profits and fortunes and refuse to abolish tax havens.The power of God’s Spirit frees us as individuals and churches to struggle in cooperation with labor unions for legal systems and economic decisions in which those able to work can find useful employment and socially meaningful jobs and— owing to increased productivity—comprehensive reduced working hours. In reaching these decisions, all of those involved in the productive process must have a voice.5. God does not want any accumulation of wealth beyond that which is necessary for life.We believe that God despises the accumulation of wealth for the few at the cost of the majority. “No one can serve two masters; for a slave will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth” (Matt. 6:24). “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or male or female slave, nor ox nor donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor” (Exod. 20:17).Therefore we reject an economic order that stimulates and rewards greed, which is dependent on nature-destroying and socially antagonistic growth, because it makes money and capital a commodity and its increase an end in itself.The Spirit of God frees us as individuals and churches to overcome the violent power of money and especially its speculative misuse as a “financial weapon of mass destruction.” We ourselves will use money at the service of economic In with social we will struggle to to money a national and international good that useful economic and to that all use of socially and to God to human through rather than through military is the of the Lord to by nor by but by the Lord of a from on is out and the a and the is a will in the and in the The of will be and the of and we say no to the of the conditions of be under any no to the more than for more than people from the causes of not they are but they are being In particular we reject the imperialist which stand in of international such as those and as well as the unlimited on we reject the of more than military under whose and such as those in the and of human and also the of the European with international the international community needs to in countries and regions because of of human this must be by under the of a power of God’s Spirit frees us as individuals and churches to refuse to cooperate in any way with in the of and we to all with to and to cooperate in and in of and to to a that to of mass destruction are believe that of mass destruction are since human beings are created in the of the of a by a human shall that be for in God’s own God (Gen. we reject the and use of means of mass which human and can even all life on earth. title: Speaking for Labor: Utah Labor News , 1917–1937
abstract: Utah's labor history has been described in terms of extremes. On the one hand, Utah's coal- and metal-mining workers made the state a center for the radical Industrial Workers of the World, or Wobblies, in the early twentieth century. On the other, the influence of the conservative Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints identified the state closely with the closed-shop movement and anticommunist crusades of the 1920s. This emphasis on the opposite poles of Utah labor can obscure the mainstream. In an attempt to broaden our understanding of Utah's labor movements, this essay offers a close reading of the Utah Labor News (ULN), the newspaper of Utah's State Federation of Labor (USFL), from 1929 to 1935. This official channel of communication provides a more nuanced picture of AFL state politics, demonstrates the variety of means unions used to reach their membership, and documents the rising tensions between craft and industrial unionists. The newspaper functioned as the mouthpiece of Utah's labor movement at a critical juncture, helping workers find their voices and articulate their demands. The goal here is principally to understand how the USFL framed contemporary issues through its official communication channels. In the process, we gain a clearer sense of the AFL's diverse membership, local differences, and wide range of political thought, particularly before 1935.Despite increased scholarly interest in labor history and labor journalism over the past decade, the role of state and local AFL-affiliated newspapers remains significantly understudied. Radical journalism tends to capture the scholarly imagination, while the AFL retains its reputation as a “conservative” organization, due to its exclusive (skilled, white, male) membership, emphasis on “business unionism,” and staunch anticommunism.1 Utah's labor press during the Great Depression suggests that it is time to revisit that interpretation.A publication under the title Utah Labor News was published in Salt Lake City from 1917 until 1920, and again from 1929 to 1944 by M. I. Thompson. From 1929 to 1935, it served as the official publication of the USFL. As such, it offers a unique window into the conditions, struggles, obstacles, and victories of Utah's labor movement, as well as the growth, policies, and problems of the USFL, all from the sympathetic perspective of labor. In 1935, due to both personal and political conflicts, the ULN lost the USFL's official endorsement, but Thompson continued to publish the newspaper until at least 1944. After 1935, the USFL endorsed both The Labor Broadcast of Salt Lake City and the Utah Trades Journal of Ogden as its official newspapers.Founded in 1904, the USFL led a precarious existence until the early 1930s. Scholars have suggested a number of reasons for this, including ruthless owner resistance to unionization of their workforce, the often at-odds political goals and strategies of the USFL's diverse members, a high immigrant population among miners, and economic instability in the mining industry.2 Indeed, the labor history of Utah is closely tied to mining. The Western Federation of Miners (WFM), a radical labor union that organized the miners and smelter workers of the Rocky Mountain states, was created in 1893. The WFM had a reputation for violent strikes and militant action, and it aroused hostility, violence, and repression from mine owners as well as state authorities and the federal government.
